RESTRICTIONS ON DISTRIBUTIONS TO SHAREHOLDERS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — RESTRICTIONS ON DISTRIBUTIONS TO SHAREHOLDERS
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., a stock corporation organized under the laws of California, and to the statutory restrictions on Acme, Inc.'s ability to make a distribution to its shareholders. It was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, Chief Financial Officer of Acme, Inc., in connection with the following distribution under consideration: $0.50 per share cash dividend to common shareholders of record.

It describes the restrictions that Chapter 5 of the California General Corporation Law (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 500-511), titled "Dividends and Reacquisitions of Shares," places on when a California corporation or its subsidiaries may make a distribution to shareholders -- including the statutory definition of "distribution to its shareholders," the alternative balance-sheet-based tests in Section 500, the separate ability-to-pay-debts test in Section 501, and the statutory consequences under Sections 316 and 506 for directors and shareholders when a distribution violates these provisions.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not calculate whether $0.50 per share cash dividend to common shareholders of record satisfies any test described below, does not determine whether Acme, Inc.'s board of directors has made or can make the good-faith determination Section 500 requires, and does not constitute legal, financial, or accounting advice regarding Acme, Inc. or any specific distribution.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "DISTRIBUTION TO ITS SHAREHOLDERS"
The restrictions described in this information sheet apply to a defined statutory term. California's General Corporation Law defines "distribution to its shareholders" as the transfer of cash or property by a corporation to its shareholders without consideration, whether by way of dividend or otherwise, except a dividend in shares of the corporation, or the purchase or redemption of its shares for cash or property -- and this includes a transfer, purchase, or redemption made by a subsidiary of the corporation, not only by the corporation itself. The statute also fixes when a distribution is deemed to occur: a distribution by way of dividend is timed to the date of declaration, and a distribution by purchase or redemption of shares is timed to the date cash or property is transferred, regardless of whether that transfer occurs under an earlier contract.

The definition excludes three narrow categories from the term "distribution to its shareholders": satisfaction of a final court judgment ordering rescission of a share issuance; a board-determined rescission of a share issuance, subject to specific board findings; and a repurchase of shares issued under Section 408, also subject to specific board findings. Each of the latter two exclusions requires the board to determine, among other things, that the corporation is likely to be able to meet its liabilities (except those otherwise adequately provided for) as they mature.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Distribution to its shareholders” means the transfer of cash or property by a corporation to its shareholders without consideration, whether by way of dividend or otherwise, except a dividend in shares of the corporation, or the purchase or redemption of its shares for cash or property, including the transfer, purchase, or redemption by a subsidiary of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 166, California General Corporation Law, definition of "distribution to its shareholders" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=166.)
  "“Distribution to its shareholders” shall not include (a) satisfaction of a final judgment of a court or tribunal of appropriate jurisdiction ordering the rescission of the issuance of shares, (b) the rescission by a corporation of the issuance of it shares, if the board determines (with any director who is, or would be, a party to the transaction not being entitled to vote) that (1) it is reasonably likely that the holder or holders of the shares in question could legally enforce a claim for the rescission, (2) that the rescission is in the best interests of the corporation, and (3) the corporation is likely to be able to meet its liabilities (except those for which payment is otherwise adequately provided) as they mature, or (c) the repurchase by a corporation of its shares issued by it pursuant to Section 408, if the board determines (with any director who is, or would be, a party to the transaction not being entitled to vote) that (1) the repurchase is in the best interests of the corporation and that (2) the corporation is likely to be able to meet its liabilities (except those for which payment is otherwise adequately provided) as they mature."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 166, California General Corporation Law, exclusions from the definition of "distribution to its shareholders" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=166.)
  Known gap: Both citations are drawn from the same statutory section (Section 166) and are not independent of one another. This clause states the statutory definition only; it does not state the separate tests in Sections 500 and 501 that govern when a transfer meeting this definition is permitted (see other clauses in this information sheet), and it does not address the sinking-fund timing rule or the debt-exchange timing rule that Section 166 also contains.

SECTION 500'S ALTERNATIVE BALANCE-SHEET TESTS
Section 500 of the California General Corporation Law restricts when a corporation, or any of its subsidiaries, may make a distribution to the corporation's shareholders. The statute does not use a single fixed test; it prohibits a distribution unless the corporation's board of directors has determined in good faith that at least one of two alternative conditions is satisfied. The first alternative is a retained-earnings test: that the corporation's retained earnings immediately before the distribution equal or exceed the sum of the proposed distribution plus the "preferential dividends arrears amount" (the amount of any cumulative, unpaid dividends owed on shares senior to the shares receiving the distribution, which the articles of incorporation can reduce to zero). The second alternative is an asset-versus-liabilities test: that immediately after the distribution, the value of the corporation's assets would equal or exceed the sum of its total liabilities plus the "preferential rights amount" (the amount that would be needed, if the corporation dissolved at the time of the distribution, to satisfy dissolution-preference rights senior to the shares receiving the distribution, which the articles can likewise reduce to zero).

As currently written, the statute does not specify a fixed numeric cushion or ratio (such as a 1.25-to-1 asset-to-liability ratio) for either alternative -- the second alternative requires assets to equal or exceed liabilities plus the preferential rights amount, without a stated multiplier. The board may base its good-faith determination under either alternative on financial statements prepared under accounting practices reasonable under the circumstances, a fair valuation, or any other method reasonable under the circumstances, and the effect of the distribution is measured as of the date it is authorized if payment occurs within 120 days of that authorization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Neither a corporation nor any of its subsidiaries shall make any distribution to the corporation’s shareholders (Section 166) unless the board of directors has determined in good faith either of the following: (1) The amount of retained earnings of the corporation immediately prior to the distribution equals or exceeds the sum of (A) the amount of the proposed distribution plus (B) the preferential dividends arrears amount. (2) Immediately after the distribution, the value of the corporation’s assets would equal or exceed the sum of its total liabilities plus the preferential rights amount."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 500(a), California General Corporation Law, the two alternative tests for a permitted distribution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=500.)
  "“preferential rights amount” means the amount that would be needed if the corporation were to be dissolved at the time of the distribution to satisfy the preferential rights, including accrued but unpaid dividends, of other shareholders upon dissolution that are superior to the rights of the shareholders receiving the distribution"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 500(b), California General Corporation Law, definition of "preferential rights amount" used in the asset-versus-liabilities test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=500.)
  "(d) The effect of a distribution under paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (a) is measured as of the date the distribution is authorized if the payment occurs within 120 days after the date of authorization."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 500(d), California General Corporation Law, timing rule for measuring a distribution's effect (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=500.)
  Known gap: All of the quoted material comes from a single statutory section (Section 500, subdivisions (a), (b), and (d)) and is not independent of one another as a source. This clause does not describe Section 500's separate rules on indebtedness issued as a distribution (subdivision (e)) or its exclusion for certain licensed broker-dealers (subdivision (f)), and it does not describe the distinct ability-to-pay-debts test in Section 501, which is covered in a separate clause. The statutory text quoted was current as of the check date above (reflecting amendments effective January 1, 2023); a reader should confirm no later amendment has changed it.

SECTION 501'S SEPARATE ABILITY-TO-PAY-DEBTS TEST
In addition to the two balance-sheet-based tests in Section 500, California's General Corporation Law imposes a separate, independently stated restriction in Section 501: neither a corporation nor any of its subsidiaries may make a distribution to the corporation's shareholders if the corporation or the subsidiary making the distribution is, or as a result of the distribution would be, likely to be unable to meet its liabilities as they mature, except liabilities whose payment is otherwise adequately provided for. This is an equitable-insolvency-style, ability-to-pay-debts test, distinct from the retained-earnings and asset-versus-liabilities tests in Section 500 -- a distribution can satisfy one or both of Section 500's balance-sheet tests and still be restricted separately by Section 501 if it would leave the corporation or subsidiary unable to meet maturing liabilities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Neither a corporation nor any of its subsidiaries shall make any distribution to the corporation’s shareholders (Section 166) if the corporation or the subsidiary making the distribution is, or as a result thereof would be, likely to be unable to meet its liabilities (except those whose payment is otherwise adequately provided for) as they mature."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 501, California General Corporation Law, restriction on distributions that would leave a corporation unable to meet maturing liabilities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=501.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses Section 501 alone, a section separately numbered from and independent of Section 500 and Section 166. It does not restate the balance-sheet tests of Section 500 (covered in a separate clause) and does not describe what accounting method or evidentiary standard a corporation must use to assess its ability to meet maturing liabilities, a point Section 501's text does not itself specify.

SECTION 316'S LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS WHO APPROVE AN UNLAWFUL DISTRIBUTION
California's General Corporation Law imposes a specific statutory consequence on directors who approve a distribution that violates Sections 500 through 503. Under Section 316, directors of a corporation who approve a distribution to shareholders that is contrary to Sections 500 to 503 are jointly and severally liable to the corporation, for the benefit of creditors or shareholders entitled to sue, up to the amount of the illegal distribution (or, for a distribution of property, its fair market value at the time of the distribution), plus interest at the legal rate on judgments from the date of the distribution, plus reasonably incurred appraisal or valuation costs -- capped at the liabilities owed to nonconsenting creditors at the time of the violation and the injury suffered by nonconsenting shareholders. A director who is present at the board (or committee) meeting where the distribution is approved and abstains from voting is treated as having approved it. A director held liable under Section 316 may compel contribution from other liable directors, and is subrogated to the corporation's rights against the shareholders who received the unlawful distribution.

Section 316's liability is expressly made "subject to the provisions of Section 309." Section 309 states the general standard of director conduct: that a director must perform the director's duties in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders, and with the care -- including reasonable inquiry -- that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances, and that a director may rely in specified circumstances on information and reports prepared by officers, employees, counsel, accountants, or board committees. Section 309 further states that a director who performs the director's duties in accordance with that standard has no liability based on an alleged failure to discharge the director's obligations as a director.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "316. (a) Subject to the provisions of Section 309, directors of a corporation who approve any of the following corporate actions shall be jointly and severally liable to the corporation for the benefit of all of the creditors or shareholders entitled to institute an action under subdivision (c): (1) The making of any distribution to its shareholders to the extent that it is contrary to the provisions of Sections 500 to 503, inclusive."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 316(a), California General Corporation Law, director liability for a distribution contrary to Sections 500-503 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=316.)
  "The damages recoverable from a director under this section shall be the amount of the illegal distribution (or if the illegal distribution consists of property, the fair market value of that property at the time of the illegal distribution) plus interest thereon from the date of the distribution at the legal rate on judgments until paid"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 316(d), California General Corporation Law, measure of damages recoverable from a liable director (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=316.)
  "(a) A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 309(a), (c), California General Corporation Law, general standard of director conduct and its liability shield (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=309.)
  Known gap: The two statutory sections cited (Section 316 and Section 309) are genuinely distinct, independently numbered General Corporation Law sections, not merely subsections of the same section -- Section 316's own text cross-references Section 309, and this clause relies on the text of both. This clause does not determine how Section 309's good-faith/reasonable-care standard applies to any specific director's conduct or any specific distribution, and does not address Section 316's separate liability provisions for post-dissolution asset distributions or unlawful loans/guaranties (subdivision (a)(2) and (3)), which concern different corporate actions than an ordinary distribution to shareholders.

SECTION 506'S LIABILITY OF A SHAREHOLDER WHO RECEIVES AN UNLAWFUL DISTRIBUTION
California's General Corporation Law also creates a specific statutory consequence for a shareholder, not only for directors. Under Section 506, a shareholder who receives a distribution prohibited by Chapter 5 (which includes distributions that violate Section 500 or Section 501) with knowledge of facts indicating the impropriety of the distribution is liable to the corporation, for the benefit of creditors or shareholders entitled to sue, for the amount received (or, for noncash property, its fair market value at the time of the illegal distribution, plus appraisal or valuation costs), with interest at the legal rate on judgments -- capped, as with director liability, at the liabilities owed to nonconsenting creditors at the time of the violation and the injury suffered by nonconsenting shareholders. A shareholder sued under Section 506 may implead other liable shareholders and compel contribution. A cause of action to recover a distribution under Section 506 is extinguished unless brought within four years of the date the distribution was made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any shareholder who receives any distribution prohibited by this chapter with knowledge of facts indicating the impropriety thereof is liable to the corporation for the benefit of all of the creditors or shareholders entitled to institute an action under subdivision (b) for the amount so received by the shareholder with interest thereon at the legal rate on judgments until paid"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 506(a), California General Corporation Law, liability of a shareholder who knowingly receives a prohibited distribution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=506.)
  "A cause of action with respect to an obligation to return a distribution pursuant to this section shall be extinguished unless the action is brought within four years after the date the distribution is made."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 506(b), California General Corporation Law, four-year limitations period for recovering an unlawful distribution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=506.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses Section 506 alone, a section separately numbered from and independent of Sections 500, 501, and 316, though it operates as part of the same statutory scheme (violations of Sections 500 or 501 trigger the liability). Section 506 conditions shareholder liability on the shareholder having received the distribution "with knowledge of facts indicating the impropriety thereof" -- this clause does not determine whether any specific shareholder had such knowledge with respect to any specific distribution, and does not describe Section 506(d)'s cross-reference to fraudulent-transfer liability under the Civil Code, which this clause has not separately verified.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause addresses Section 506 alone, a section separately numbered from and independent of Sections 500, 501, and 316, though it operates as part of the same statutory scheme (violations of Sections 500 or 501 trigger the liability). Section 506 conditions shareholder liability on the shareholder having received the distribution "with knowledge of facts indicating the impropriety thereof" -- this clause does not determine whether any specific shareholder had such knowledge with respect to any specific distribution, and does not describe Section 506(d)'s cross-reference to fraudulent-transfer liability under the Civil Code, which this clause has not separately verified.

Distribution under consideration by Acme, Inc.: $0.50 per share cash dividend to common shareholders of record

This worksheet is provided to organize -- not to perform or certify -- the good-faith determination Section 500 asks a corporation's board of directors to make, and the separate assessment Section 501 asks the corporation to make, before Acme, Inc. makes the distribution described above. Each line below identifies an input the statutes described in this information sheet reference; it does not supply a value, a conclusion, or a recommendation.

☐ Amount of the proposed distribution described above.
☐ Retained earnings of Acme, Inc. immediately prior to the proposed distribution.
☐ Preferential dividends arrears amount (cumulative unpaid dividends on any shares senior to the shares that would receive this distribution), if any, or a note that the articles of incorporation set this amount at zero.
☐ Value of Acme, Inc.'s assets immediately after the proposed distribution, and the method used to value them (financial statements, fair valuation, or another stated method).
☐ Total liabilities of Acme, Inc. immediately after the proposed distribution.
☐ Preferential rights amount (dissolution-preference rights senior to the shares that would receive this distribution), if any, or a note that the articles of incorporation set this amount at zero.
☐ Assessment of whether Acme, Inc. is, or as a result of the proposed distribution would be, likely to be unable to meet its liabilities as they mature (except liabilities otherwise adequately provided for).
☐ Date the proposed distribution is authorized, and date payment is expected to occur.

This information sheet regarding Acme, Inc. was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, Chief Financial Officer.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________
Title: Chief Financial Officer

[This information sheet describes the distribution-restriction statutes in Cal. Corp. Code §§ 166, 500, 501, 309, 316, and 506 -- the statutory definition of "distribution to its shareholders," the alternative balance-sheet tests and the separate ability-to-pay-debts test that restrict when a distribution may be made, and the statutory consequences for directors and shareholders when a distribution violates these provisions. It does not itself make the good-faith determination Section 500 requires of Acme, Inc.'s board of directors, does not certify compliance with Section 501, and does not constitute legal, financial, or accounting advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]
